name: Sara Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes out with your name on it. I'll describe five pictures of the future and ask what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hollis Superstore, the huge one by the ring road, split between the deli counter and the tills. Mornings I'm slicing ham and weighing olives, afternoons I'm on till nine. I'm still the new one on the deli, so the older ladies check my labels, and fair enough, I've mixed up the cheese prices more than once. I like the deli more, you actually talk to people about what they're cooking.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and how are things at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The slicer cleaning at closing wears me out, it takes forty minutes and you smell of salami all night. Home's good, my partner Ben is a plumber and we rent a two-bed near the park. We're saving for a house, about eight months of costs put away, plus Ben's van is paid off. Hollis pays a deli rate and Sunday extra, so it's decent money for what it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then, back to normal. At work we'd laugh about the AI label printer that still prints the wrong cheese. I'm not big online, maybe a comment in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we stay on track for the house. My job's steady, Ben's is steady. The only real question is whether I stay on the deli or try something with more of a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep both my shifts and keep saving for the deposit, maybe buy in eighteen months. I'd look at the pharmacy assistant course, because Hollis has an in-store pharmacy and Mrs Okoro, the pharmacist, said they need people. I'd want to hear from someone who's done it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty content. It's the life we'd planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to hear from someone first. Who would you ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Jo did a pharmacy course two years ago and works at a chemist in town. I'd buy Jo a coffee and ask her straight whether it's worth the evenings. If Jo says yes, I'd sign up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a part of the deli job you'd miss if you moved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Christmas rush, weirdly. Everyone's ordering hams and cheese boards and it's chaos but happy chaos. I'd miss the regulars asking what's good this week.

say: I'd say it's **back to normal**, and joke about the label printer.
I'd leave a short comment in the **group chat**, not much more.
think: We stay on track for the **house**, with both jobs steady.
The real question is whether the deli has **a future** for me.
do: Keep saving to buy a house in about **eighteen months**.
Ask my friend Jo about the **pharmacy assistant** course before signing up.
Keep both my **deli and till** shifts.
feel: **Calm** and content, living the life we'd planned.
S0.quote: The only real question is whether I stay on the deli or try something with more of a future.
fieldNote: Her life plan centres on **buying a house** with Ben.
She checks with a **friend who's done it** before changing course.
She enjoys the **human side** of the deli counter.

steps.text: Keep saving monthly toward a house deposit
Ask Jo about the pharmacy assistant course over coffee
Keep the deli and till shifts at Hollis

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to adapt, and Hollis will probably handle it okay because it's big. I'd tell people at work to learn the new systems instead of moaning. Online I'd stay quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My deli and till work changes slowly, robots are slow here. But head office would use AI for ordering and rotas, so the managers would change before us. I'd worry more about where the deli is in five years, if self-service grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the pharmacy assistant course this year, two evenings a week. I'd learn the new rota app properly, I already use AI to plan holidays sometimes. We'd still buy a house, but maybe a cheaper one so we have a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared. Like hearing a noise in the car that hasn't become a problem yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't a pharmacy job change too, with AI checking prescriptions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the checking bit, yes. But someone still has to talk to the customer and hand over the bag. I'd ask Mrs Okoro straight out what she thinks before I commit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the deli?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margaret, who's been on the deli eleven years and checks all my labels. If the superstore cut the deli to one person per shift, I think they'd keep my colleague Margaret and not me. And honestly, that'd be right.

say: I'd say adapting is **sensible**, and big shops like **Hollis** will cope.
I'd tell colleagues to **learn the new systems** instead of moaning.
think: My work changes slowly, but **managers** feel AI first.
I'd worry where the **deli** is in five years if self-service grows.
do: Start the **pharmacy assistant** course, two evenings a week.
Buy a **cheaper house** to keep a cushion.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a noise in the car that isn't a problem yet.
S1.quote: If the superstore cut the deli to one person per shift, I think they'd keep my colleague Margaret and not me. And honestly, that'd be right.
fieldNote: She's **honest** about being junior and likely first to go.
She checks the pharmacy plan with **Mrs Okoro** before committing.
She trims the house plan to a **cheaper** buy as a hedge.

steps.text: Enrol in the pharmacy assistant course, two evenings a week
Learn the new Hollis rota app properly
Look at cheaper houses so savings stay as a cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and the government should make firms slow down. At work I'd say we need to stick together and ask Hollis what the plan is. I'd still not post much, it's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the pharmacy idea dies, because AGI by 2028 does the checking and advice. Then robots by 2031 do the deli and tills. So I'd have about three years in a job that's going anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pause the house, for a year at least, because I wouldn't take a mortgage on two shaky jobs. I'd ask Ben about joining his plumbing work, maybe doing his bookings first and then training as his apprentice. Plumbing is hands-on, so it gets those extra years before robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Ben would say it's fine and I'd believe him for about a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Doing Ben's bookings sounds like thinking work. Wouldn't AI take that in 2028 too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You're right, the bookings would go to AI fast. So it would have to be the actual pipes, under sinks with a torch. I'm not sure I want that, but I'd rather be under a sink than out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday to Ben's sister's in the summer, and eating out on Fridays. We'd keep the savings for the house, just not spend them yet. I'd rather have the money sitting there doing nothing than gone.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and firms should be made to slow down.
I'd ask **Hollis** directly what its plan is for staff.
think: The **pharmacy idea dies**, because AGI by 2028 does checking and advice.
I'd have about **three years** in a job that's going anyway.
do: **Pause the house** purchase for at least a year.
Train as Ben's **plumbing apprentice**, doing the actual pipe work.
Cut the **summer holiday** and Friday meals out.
feel: **Anxious**, only half believing Ben when he says it's fine.
S2.quote: I'd rather be under a sink than out of work.
fieldNote: She sees thinking AI **closes the pharmacy route** before robots arrive.
She shifts toward **hands-on plumbing** to use the 3-year gap.
She'd keep savings **unspent** rather than gamble on a house.

steps.text: Put the house purchase on hold for a year
Start training as Ben's plumbing apprentice
Cancel the summer trip and Friday meals out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but doable if we're smart. I'd tell friends to look at hands-on trades. I'd sound calmer than I feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means AI takes the thinking stuff by 2031 and robots come for the deli around 2034. That's long enough to learn plumbing properly, and Ben could teach me. But it's the same ending, just slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a plumbing course at the college next year and help Ben on Saturdays to learn. I'd keep my Hollis shifts for the first year or two. We'd buy a smaller house, maybe in two years, once I'm qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. Having a plan helps me sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't you and Ben both be in plumbing, and both exposed to robots later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's the risk. My partner Ben and I would both be in plumbing, all eggs in one van. But plumbing in old houses is fiddly, every job's different. If robots can do that, then everyone's in trouble anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Margaret at the deli?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Margaret about the five years and say she might make it to retirement. Margaret's 59, so she probably would. I'd be glad for her.

say: I'd tell friends to look at **hands-on trades**.
I'd say five years is **short but doable**, sounding calmer than I feel.
think: Robots reach the deli **around 2034**, enough time to learn plumbing.
It's the **same ending** as the fast one, just slower and easier to plan.
do: Start a **plumbing course** at the college next year.
Help Ben on **Saturdays** to learn the trade.
Keep my **Hollis shifts** for a year or two.
feel: **Anxious** but busy, and the plan helps me **sleep**.
S3.quote: My partner Ben and I would both be in plumbing, all eggs in one van.
fieldNote: She spots the risk of **both partners** in one trade.
She expects old-house plumbing to be **hard to automate**.
She is glad for **Margaret**, who may reach retirement.

steps.text: Enrol in the college plumbing course next year
Work Saturdays alongside Ben on plumbing jobs
Keep the Hollis deli shifts for two years
Buy a smaller house once qualified

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fine, we can plan properly. I'd tell people at work to use the time, not ignore it. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means the house goes ahead, the course goes ahead, and I'd be 37 when robots can do hands-on work. I'd probably end up in plumbing with Ben, or in the pharmacy for a while first. It's the same end point but a lot less rushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house next year as planned. I'd do the pharmacy course first, because it's proven and Jo likes it, then maybe plumbing later. I'd use AI tools a bit more at work as they come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but okay. It feels far enough off to live our life first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep the pharmacy idea here but dropped it in the fast version. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with ten years the pharmacy job still has a good run before AGI. Six or seven years of decent work in the pharmacy is worth it. In the fast one it'd be over before I'd finished training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have children sooner or later in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably about when we'd planned, in a few years. I'd want the house first. Ten years doesn't change that much.

say: I'd say ten years lets us **plan properly**.
I'd tell colleagues to **use the time**, not ignore it.
think: The **house and course** both go ahead, much less rushed.
I'd be **37** when robots can do hands-on work.
do: **Buy the house** next year as planned.
Do the **pharmacy course** first, since it's proven.
Consider **plumbing with Ben** later in the decade.
feel: **Uneasy but okay**, far enough off to live our life first.
S4.quote: Six or seven years of decent work in the pharmacy is worth it.
fieldNote: The warning time decides **which retraining** makes sense for her.
Family plans like **children** stay on their original schedule.
She sticks with **proven paths**, like her friend Jo's.

steps.text: Buy the house with Ben next year
Try new AI tools at Hollis as they arrive

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it kills the pharmacy idea and the deli at the same time. What would help is cheap evening courses in real trades and some honesty from Hollis about when the robots are coming. We'd plan around it if we knew.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about couples. Ben and I decide everything together, and his job changes my answers. Nobody plans a career on their own when they're saving for a house.

headlineQuote: Nobody plans a career on their own when they're saving for a house.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old** deli and till worker at a large superstore by the ring road.
She and her partner Ben, a plumber, have **eight months saved** and want to buy a house.
She changes course once someone she trusts has **proven** it works.
She's calm in AI Plateau, uneasy in Steady Disruption, and **anxious** in the faster AGI pictures.
Warning time decides her route: **pharmacy** if there's time, **plumbing** if not.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which closes the pharmacy route and the deli at once.
whatWouldHelp: Honest notice from Hollis about **when robots arrive**.
